definition: Deoxyribonucleic acid — the molecule that carries genetic information in the form of a sequence of bases.
A section of DNA that codes for a specific protein, which determines a characteristic.
The complete set of genetic information (DNA) of an organism.
A long strand of coiled DNA found in the nucleus, carrying many genes.
A different version of the same gene, e.g. the gene for eye colour has alleles for blue and brown.
An allele that is always expressed in the phenotype, even if only one copy is present. Represented by a capital letter.
An allele that is only expressed in the phenotype when two copies are present (homozygous recessive). Represented by a lowercase letter.
Having two identical alleles for a gene, e.g. BB or bb.
Having two different alleles for a gene, e.g. Bb.
The genetic makeup of an organism — the alleles it carries, e.g. Bb.
The observable characteristics of an organism resulting from its genotype and environment.
A diagram used to predict the possible genotypes and phenotypes of offspring from a genetic cross.
A sex cell (sperm or egg) that contains half the normal number of chromosomes (haploid).
The fusion of a male gamete (sperm) and a female gamete (egg) to form a zygote.
A cell containing half the normal number of chromosomes (23 in humans). Gametes are haploid.
A cell containing the full number of chromosomes (46 in humans, in 23 pairs). Body cells are diploid.
A type of cell division that produces four genetically different haploid gametes from one diploid cell.
An inherited disorder caused by a recessive allele that causes thick mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system.
An inherited disorder caused by a dominant allele that results in extra fingers or toes.
In humans, sex is determined by the sex chromosomes: XX = female, XY = male.
Differences between individuals of the same species, which can be genetic, environmental or both.
Variation that shows a range of values with no distinct categories, e.g. height or mass.
Variation that falls into distinct categories with no intermediate values, e.g. blood group or tongue rolling.
A random change in the DNA sequence of an organism that may alter the protein produced.
The change in the inherited characteristics of a population over many generations through the process of natural selection.
The process by which individuals with advantageous characteristics are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles.
The idea that organisms best adapted to their environment are most likely to survive and reproduce.
The process by which humans select organisms with desirable characteristics and breed them together over many generations.
The process of modifying the genome of an organism by inserting a gene from another organism to give it a desired characteristic.
Human insulin is now produced by inserting the human insulin gene into bacteria, which then produce it in large quantities.
The preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms found in rock, used as evidence for evolution.
The permanent disappearance of all members of a species from the Earth.
An example of natural selection where bacteria with resistant mutations survive antibiotic treatment and reproduce, spreading resistance.
Charles Darwin — the scientist who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection after his voyage on the Beagle.
The organisation of living organisms into groups based on their characteristics and evolutionary relationships.
The system of giving organisms a two-part Latin name — genus and species — e.g. Homo sapiens.
A diagram showing the evolutionary relationships between different species based on their common ancestors.
The process by which new species form when populations become isolated and evolve separately over time.
